title: Shaking Hands with Fidel Castro
author: Nick Estes
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screen-
Shot-2026-07-30-at-9.27.05-AM-680x849.png)

William Buffalo Tiger, Chief of the Miccosukees, 1920-2015.

The State Department’s recent report alleging Cuba’s support for left-wing
“terrorism” in the United States signals a chilling escalation, as the Trump
administration draws up enemy lists for a revived Red Scare. Ultimately, the
document reads as an unwitting confession of U.S. foreign policy failure.
While the State Department celebrates how mid-century McCarthyism crushed the
“old” communist left, it inadvertently exposes Washington’s inability to
contain the “new left” and modern movements condemning U.S. aggression toward
Cuba. Even after decades of suffocating sanctions and a relentless blockade,
Cuba endures as the primary driver and “spiritual hub of the Third World
revolution,” according to the report. Crucially, as Charisse Burden-Stelley
points out, the report exposes how the U.S. ruling class racializes domestic
dissidents—framing internal struggles for liberation as foreign-directed
subversion by an external communist menace. The report frames Black freedom
movements in particular—from the Civil Rights Movement and Black Power to the
George Floyd uprising—as especially susceptible to Cuban influence, as if
racial terror were conjured by outside agitators rather than the white power
establishment itself.

This racialized paternalism extends beyond Black liberation to Indigenous
resistance as well. While the focus is primarily on Black and explicitly
communist and socialist organizations, Indigenous peoples are mentioned twice
in passing as part of the supposed Cuban plot to overthrow the United States.
The first comes from a speech by William Kunstler, an attorney for the Wounded
Knee Legal Defense/Offense Committee and National Lawyers Guild (NLG), who
mentions AIM among the “revolutionaries” he defends to keep them “functioning”
on the streets. The second involves NLG lawyers traveling to Standing Rock
during the Indigenous-led movement to stop the Dakota Access Pipeline in 2016.
Both instances mention Indigenous movements only through their representation
by non-Native and mostly white allies. The implication, as was the case with
the lawsuit against Greenpeace’s role in the Standing Rock movement, is that
Indigenous peoples cannot lead their own movements or form their own
strategies but are merely passive vehicles or unwitting dupes of outside
agitators.

Yet this dismissive narrative erases a long history of Indigenous nations
strategically turning Cold War anxieties against Washington to assert their
own sovereignty. In 1961, as Cold War anxieties gripped the continent two
years after Fidel Castro took power, a small tribal nation deep in the heat of
the Florida Everglades saw an unexpected pathway opening. For William Buffalo
Tiger, leader of the Miccosukees, the crisis was existential: federal
bureaucrats refused to acknowledge his people as a distinct nation, lumping
them under the umbrella of the larger Seminole tribe and leaving them without
a scrap of legally recognized land or the authority to rule themselves. Every
appeal to Washington met a wall of indifference. So he pursued a daring
action.

A legal advisor pitched a bold strategy: force Washington’s hand by securing
recognition from a foreign power. Partnering with his friend Wallace “Mad
Bear” Anderson—a fierce Tuscarora nationalist—Buffalo Tiger assembled ten
Miccosukee delegates. Together, they drove to the tip of Key West and boarded
a commuter plane bound for Havana on what Buffalo Tiger publicly framed as “a
goodwill delegation.”

In Cuba, officials chauffeured the group through capital streets, flanked by
guards cradling submachine guns. On their second day, they joined a sprawling
crowd in a public square, listening as Fidel Castro thundered through a six-
hour speech translated by an interpreter. Afterwards, Castro met the delegates
face-to-face, leaning in to absorb the story of their struggle. “Remember,
when you have no place to live, come here,” Castro said. He offered them
tracts of Cuban land and officially recognized the Miccosukee as a sovereign
nation.

When the delegation returned home, Buffalo Tiger’s phone rang endlessly.
Castro’s handshake had panicked Washington. FBI agents grilled the delegates
about the revolutionary government. Yet the gamble paid off. Terrified of the
diplomatic embarrassment of a small tribe allying with Havana under their
noses, federal officials fast-tracked the tribe’s petition. The Miccosukee
gained official federal recognition the following year.

The victory was nearly unthinkable against the backdrop of the era. Under the
banner of Indian termination policy, Congress had spent nearly a decade
stripping 109 tribes of their legal status, tearing up historic treaties, and
throwing millions of acres of tribal land onto the auction block. In the grip
of Red Scare mania, McCarthyite politicians vilified reservations as
dangerous, “un-American” communes. They argued that dismantling communal
tribal lands was the only way to assimilate Indigenous people into the
capitalist market—a strategy designed to pass those lands directly into white
hands. They attacked collective tribal structures as inherently socialist
threats, weaponizing anti-communist hysteria to mask blatant land grabs.

Buffalo Tiger’s trip to Cuba initiated a long-standing relationship between
Red Power activists and the Cuban revolution in subsequent decades.
Consequently, the state’s persistent red-baiting of Indigenous activists as
communist dupes sought to delegitimize a burgeoning radical sovereignty
movement. The lesson, however, is that Indigenous diplomacy and radical
internationalism have been effective mechanisms to leverage Indigenous treaty
rights and sovereignty internally within the U.S. empire. It has also exposed
the very thing that the authors of the recent Cuba report fear most: a budding
consciousness wherein Indigenous peoples within the imperial core increasingly
recognize their strength and power not by aligning with their masters, but by
building active solidarity with the poor, working classes of the global
majority who are fighting to build alternatives to the ravages of global
capitalism and U.S. imperialism.

Ultimately, whether in 1961 or the present day, the ruling class’s playbook
remains unchanged: treat imperialism and colonialism as non-issues and frame
domestic resistance as foreign subversion. By pathologizing Indigenous
sovereignty and Black liberation as products of external puppet masters, the
ruling class attempts to deny the legitimacy of internal struggle—and, more
importantly, conceal their unwillingness and inability to offer a viable
alternative beyond the exploitative machinery of racial capitalism and
imperial control. Yet history demonstrates the exact opposite. Far from being
passive victims of foreign manipulation, Black and Indigenous revolutionaries
have repeatedly exercised sophisticated political agency—wielding global anti-
imperialist ties not out of indoctrination, but as strategic self-defense
against state terror.
